stem: Who has the authority to sign a contract that binds the Government?

options.text: A warranted contracting officer acting within the limits of the warrant
options.why: Only contracting officers may enter into contracts, and only within the authority delegated to them in writing.

options.text: The commander of the requiring activity
options.why: Rank and command give no contracting authority.

options.text: The contracting officer's representative (COR)
options.why: A COR monitors performance but has no authority to sign or change contracts.

options.text: The resource manager who certified the funds
options.why: Certifying funds is not the same as authority to obligate the Government by contract.

stem: Which action is within a COR's authority?

options.text: Monitoring the contractor's technical performance and reporting to the contracting officer
options.why: That is the COR's job: watch, inspect, document and report.

options.text: Approving the contractor's request for a later delivery date
options.why: Changing delivery terms is a contract change only the contracting officer can make.

options.text: Directing extra work when the customer has spare funds
options.why: Directing new work is a change; a COR who does it may create an unauthorized commitment.

options.text: Signing small modifications under $25,000
options.why: CORs cannot sign modifications at any dollar value.

stem: When contract administration is delegated to another office, which contracting officer usually administers the contract?

options.text: The administrative contracting officer (ACO)
options.why: An ACO in a contract administration office, such as DCMA, administers delegated contracts.

options.text: The procuring contracting officer (PCO)
options.why: The PCO awards the contract; after delegation, administration moves to the ACO.

options.text: The termination contracting officer (TCO)
options.why: A TCO settles terminations, not routine administration.

options.text: The source selection authority (SSA)
options.why: The SSA chooses the winner in a source selection; it does not administer contracts.

stem: Under the FAR's guiding principles, the acquisition team may use a strategy or practice the FAR does not address when it is:

options.text: In the Government's best interest and not prohibited by law, regulation or the FAR
options.why: This is the FAR's permission principle: silence is not a prohibition.

options.text: Approved in writing in advance by the head of the contracting activity
options.why: No general advance approval is required for practices that are not prohibited.

options.text: Previously upheld by GAO in a protest decision
options.why: GAO precedent is helpful but not a condition for using a practice.

options.text: Already used by another federal agency
options.why: Another agency's use is not the test.

stem: Who normally defines the requirement and provides the funds for a buy?

options.text: The requiring activity (the customer)
options.why: The customer knows the need, writes the requirement documents and supplies certified funds.

options.text: The contracting officer
options.why: The contracting officer helps shape the requirement but does not own the need or the money.

options.text: The Defense Contract Audit Agency
options.why: DCAA audits contractor costs; it does not define requirements.

options.text: The small business professional
options.why: The small business professional advises on set-asides, not on what to buy.

stem: Which behavior best supports an effective acquisition team?

options.text: Bringing in the customer, legal, finance and small business early and sharing information
options.why: The FAR treats the acquisition team as a partnership that works best when everyone is involved early.

options.text: Keeping the customer out of contracting decisions to protect integrity
options.why: The customer is part of the team; integrity comes from following the rules, not from shutting them out.

options.text: Letting the incumbent contractor write the next requirement to save time
options.why: That creates a conflict of interest and limits competition.

options.text: Deciding the contract type before talking with the customer
options.why: Contract type depends on the requirement and its risks, which the customer helps define.

stem: Which kind of authority never binds the Government?

options.text: Apparent authority
options.why: Unlike private business, the Government is not bound by someone who only appears to have authority.

options.text: Express actual authority
options.why: Authority actually given in writing, such as in a warrant, does bind the Government.

options.text: Implied actual authority
options.why: Authority that is an integral part of duties actually assigned can bind the Government.

options.text: Authority stated on an SF 1402
options.why: The SF 1402 is the warrant itself: real, express authority.

stem: What is an unauthorized commitment?

options.text: An agreement that is not binding only because the Government person who made it lacked authority
options.why: That is the definition; the classic example is a customer ordering from a vendor without a contracting officer.

options.text: Any contract awarded without full and open competition
options.why: Sole-source awards made properly by a contracting officer are binding.

options.text: A contract signed above the contracting officer's warrant that the HCA approved in advance
options.why: Advance approval is not ratification, and the description does not match the definition.

options.text: A verbal order placed by a warranted contracting officer
options.why: A warranted contracting officer acting within authority does not create an unauthorized commitment.

stem: Under the RFO FAR, who may ratify an unauthorized commitment?

options.text: The head of the contracting activity, with delegation allowed no lower than the chief of the contracting office
options.why: FAR 1.405(b)(2) gives ratification authority to the HCA and limits how far it can be delegated.

options.text: The person who made the commitment, once funds are found
options.why: The person without authority cannot fix the problem by ratifying their own act.

options.text: The COR assigned to the contract
options.why: CORs have no contracting authority at all.

options.text: Any warranted contracting officer
options.why: Ratification is held at a higher level than an individual contracting officer.

stem: Which is NOT one of the conditions for ratifying an unauthorized commitment?

options.text: The person who made the commitment has since received a warrant
options.why: That is not a condition. The conditions concern the Government's benefit, authority, propriety, price, legal review and funds.

options.text: The Government has received the supplies or services
options.why: This is a condition: the Government must have accepted the benefit.

options.text: The price is fair and reasonable
options.why: This is a condition for ratification.

options.text: Funds were available when the commitment was made
options.why: This is a condition: proper funds must have been available at the time.

stem: Which form appoints a contracting officer and states the limits of the authority?

options.text: SF 1402, Certificate of Appointment
options.why: The SF 1402 is the warrant.

options.text: SF 30, Amendment of Solicitation/Modification of Contract
options.why: The SF 30 is used for amendments and modifications.

options.text: SF 1449, Solicitation/Contract/Order for Commercial Products and Commercial Services
options.why: The SF 1449 is a commercial solicitation and contract form.

options.text: DD 1155, Order for Supplies or Services
options.why: The DD 1155 is a purchase or delivery order form.

stem: Before signing a contract, the contracting officer must make sure that:

options.text: All legal and regulatory requirements are met and sufficient funds are available
options.why: These are among the contracting officer's core responsibilities.

options.text: The contractor has waived its right to appeal disputes
options.why: Contractors keep their Contract Disputes Act rights; no waiver is required.

options.text: The COR has inspected the contractor's facility
options.why: Facility inspections are not a general requirement before signing.

options.text: GAO has reviewed the solicitation
options.why: GAO reviews protests; it does not pre-approve solicitations.

stem: What is the DFARS?

options.text: The Department of War supplement to the FAR
options.why: DFARS adds DoW-specific rules that implement and supplement the FAR.

options.text: The Army's supplement to the FAR
options.why: That is the AFARS.

options.text: A governmentwide regulation that replaces the FAR
options.why: Supplements add to the FAR; they do not replace it.

options.text: Guidance with no regulatory force
options.why: That describes the PGI, not the DFARS.

stem: In the citation FAR 15.404-1(b), what does 15.4 refer to?

options.text: Subpart 15.4
options.why: The part number, a decimal point and the next digit form the subpart.

options.text: Section 15.404
options.why: 15.404 is the section within the subpart.

options.text: Paragraph (b)
options.why: (b) is the paragraph.

options.text: FAR Part 4
options.why: The part is 15; the 4 identifies the subpart within Part 15.

stem: The Army's supplement to the FAR and DFARS is the:

options.text: AFARS
options.why: The Army Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement, numbered 5101 to 5153.

options.text: DFARS PGI
options.why: PGI is DoW-wide guidance that accompanies the DFARS.

options.text: GSAR
options.why: The GSAR is the General Services Administration's supplement.

options.text: OMB Circular A-76
options.why: A-76 concerns public-private competition, not FAR supplementation.

stem: A class deviation applies to:

options.text: A category of contract actions
options.why: Class deviations cover more than one action, such as all actions of a certain kind.

options.text: A single contract action
options.why: That is an individual deviation.

options.text: Only actions above the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: Class deviations are not limited by dollar value.

options.text: Only contracts with foreign companies
options.why: Class deviations can cover any category of actions.

stem: Since when has DoW used the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO) parts through class deviations?

options.text: 1 February 2026
options.why: DoW's RFO class deviations, with matching DFARS changes, took effect 1 February 2026.

options.text: 1 October 2025
options.why: That was the date of the inflation adjustment to thresholds, not DoW's RFO effective date.

options.text: 15 April 2025
options.why: April 2025 is when the executive order launching the overhaul was signed.

options.text: DoW has not adopted any RFO parts
options.why: DoW adopted them through class deviations while formal rulemaking continues.

stem: What is the title of FAR Part 42?

options.text: Contract Administration and Audit Services
options.why: Part 42 covers administration, audit services, novation, stop-work orders and past performance reporting.

options.text: Contract Modifications
options.why: That is Part 43.

options.text: Subcontracting Policies and Procedures
options.why: That is Part 44.

options.text: Quality Assurance
options.why: That is Part 46.

stem: In a request for quotations (RFQ), what is the vendor's quotation?

options.text: Not an offer; the Government's purchase order is the offer
options.why: A quote is information. A contract forms when the vendor accepts the Government's order in writing or by performing.

options.text: An offer that the Government accepts by issuing a purchase order
options.why: That describes proposals under an RFP, not quotes under an RFQ.

options.text: Binding on the vendor for 60 days
options.why: A quote does not bind the vendor.

options.text: An acceptance of the Government's RFQ
options.why: An RFQ is a request for information, not an offer to accept.

stem: Which is NOT an essential element of a contract?

options.text: A signature from the COR
options.why: CORs do not sign contracts; their signature is not an element of contract formation.

options.text: Consideration
options.why: Each party must give something of value.

options.text: Offer and acceptance
options.why: Mutual agreement on the same terms is essential.

options.text: A lawful purpose
options.why: A contract for an unlawful purpose is not enforceable.

stem: The Government wants to transfer money to a university to carry out a public purpose, and Government staff will be substantially involved. Which instrument fits?

options.text: A cooperative agreement
options.why: Substantial Government involvement in carrying out a public purpose is what separates a cooperative agreement from a grant.

options.text: A grant
options.why: A grant is used when no substantial Government involvement is expected.

options.text: A contract
options.why: A contract is for buying property or services for the Government's direct benefit or use.

options.text: A purchase order
options.why: A purchase order is a type of contract.

stem: A vendor replies to your purchase order: 'Accepted, but delivery will be 60 days instead of 30.' What is this?

options.text: A counteroffer, so no contract exists on the original terms
options.why: An acceptance must match the offer. Changing a material term is a counteroffer.

options.text: An acceptance with a minor change that binds both sides
options.why: Delivery time is material; changing it is not an acceptance.

options.text: A protest
options.why: A protest objects to a solicitation or award; this is a reply to an order.

options.text: A constructive change
options.why: Constructive changes happen after a contract exists, through Government actions.

stem: Which statement about a blanket purchase agreement (BPA) is correct?

options.text: The BPA is not a contract; each call placed under it is
options.why: A BPA sets terms in advance; obligations arise when calls are placed.

options.text: Signing the BPA obligates the full estimated amount
options.why: A BPA obligates nothing by itself.

options.text: A BPA is a kind of grant
options.why: A BPA is an acquisition tool, not financial assistance.

options.text: A BPA can be used only for services
options.why: BPAs are used for supplies and services.

stem: Which statement about other transactions (OTs) is correct?

options.text: They are not governed by the FAR and are used only under specific statutory authority
options.why: OTs, such as prototype agreements under 10 U.S.C. 4022, are outside the FAR.

options.text: They are a type of FAR-based contract
options.why: OTs are not FAR contracts.

options.text: They are used only for construction
options.why: OTs are mainly used for research and prototypes.

options.text: They are the same as grants
options.why: Grants are a separate assistance instrument.

stem: The bona fide needs rule deals with which leg of fiscal law?

options.text: Time
options.why: It requires that funds pay for needs of the period the appropriation is available.

options.text: Purpose
options.why: Purpose is about what the money may be spent on (31 U.S.C. 1301).

options.text: Amount
options.why: Amount is about not exceeding what is available (Antideficiency Act).

options.text: Competition
options.why: Competition is a contracting rule, not a fiscal law leg.

stem: DoW operation and maintenance (O&M) funds are generally available for new obligations for how long?

options.text: 1 year
options.why: O&M is a one-year appropriation.

options.text: 2 years
options.why: Two years is typical for RDT&E.

options.text: 3 years
options.why: Three years is typical for procurement.

options.text: 5 years
options.why: Five years is typical for military construction.

stem: Obligating more money than an appropriation makes available violates the:

options.text: Antideficiency Act
options.why: The Act prohibits obligating or spending in excess of, or in advance of, available appropriations.

options.text: Procurement Integrity Act
options.why: That Act protects procurement information and limits employment contacts.

options.text: Truthful Cost or Pricing Data statute
options.why: That statute concerns certified cost or pricing data.

options.text: Prompt Payment Act
options.why: That Act concerns paying contractors on time.

stem: A modification will add work and $40,000 to a contract. When may the contracting officer sign it?

options.text: Only after funds are available for the added cost
options.why: Contracting officers may not execute modifications that increase obligations without available funds.

options.text: Before funds, if the contractor agrees to wait to be paid
options.why: The contractor's agreement does not cure an obligation without funds.

options.text: Whenever the COR approves the added work
options.why: COR approval is not funding and not authority.

options.text: After the contractor finishes the added work
options.why: Obligating after the fact does not fix the timing problem; funds must come first.

stem: A unit wants to use O&M funds to build a large new permanent building that requires military construction funds. Which leg of fiscal law is the problem?

options.text: Purpose
options.why: Using one appropriation for something Congress funds through another is a purpose violation.

options.text: Time
options.why: The issue is not the fiscal year of the need.

options.text: Amount
options.why: The issue is not exceeding available money.

options.text: Competition
options.why: Competition is a contracting rule, not a fiscal law leg.

stem: Which clause lets the Government award a contract before funds are available, with no Government liability until funds are made available?

options.text: 52.232-18, Availability of Funds
options.why: It conditions the Government's obligation on funds becoming available.

options.text: 52.232-22, Limitation of Funds
options.why: That clause manages incremental funding on cost-type contracts.

options.text: 52.243-1, Changes
options.why: That clause covers changes to fixed-price contracts.

options.text: 52.249-14, Excusable Delays
options.why: That clause covers delays beyond the contractor's control.

stem: Under the Procurement Integrity Act, before award you may not disclose:

options.text: Contractor bid or proposal information and source selection information
options.why: The Act bars disclosing these to anyone not authorized to receive them.

options.text: The solicitation's closing date
options.why: The closing date is public information in the solicitation.

options.text: The name of the contracting officer
options.why: The contracting officer's name appears in the solicitation.

options.text: The solicitation number
options.why: The solicitation number is public.

stem: You are working personally and substantially on a $2 million competition. An offeror asks you about a job. What must you do?

options.text: Report the contact, and either reject the employment offer or disqualify yourself from the buy
options.why: For procurements above the SAT, the Procurement Integrity Act requires reporting and a choice to reject or recuse.

options.text: Nothing, as long as you do not accept until after award
options.why: The duty to report and decide applies when the contact happens.

options.text: Tell the other offerors so the process stays fair
options.why: That does not meet the reporting rule and shares information improperly.

options.text: Ask the offeror to call back after award
options.why: Deferring the conversation does not satisfy the requirement to report and decide.

stem: FAR 3.101 requires Government business to be conducted:

options.text: Above reproach, with complete impartiality and preferential treatment for none
options.why: That is the general standard of conduct.

options.text: As fast as possible, whatever the cost
options.why: Speed does not override integrity and fairness.

options.text: With a preference for incumbent contractors
options.why: Preferential treatment for anyone is prohibited.

options.text: With a preference for local vendors
options.why: Preferences exist only where law provides them, not by personal choice.

stem: During an open competition, the incumbent's manager invites you to lunch to 'talk about the requirement.' What is the best response?

options.text: Decline and ask them to submit questions in writing to the contracting officer
options.why: That avoids a gift from a prohibited source and unequal access to information.

options.text: Accept if the lunch costs under $20
options.why: Even if a gift rule exception might apply, private meetings during a competition give one firm an unfair advantage.

options.text: Accept if you pay your own share
options.why: Paying removes the gift problem but not the unequal-access problem.

options.text: Accept if the contracting officer comes too
options.why: Questions about an open competition belong in writing so every offeror gets the same answers.

stem: Several firms submit identical bids on repeated buys of the same item. What should you do?

options.text: Treat it as a possible sign of collusion and report it through legal counsel
options.why: Identical bids can indicate bid rigging, which is reported for possible antitrust violations.

options.text: Treat it as proof of adequate price competition
options.why: Identical bids can mean the firms are not competing independently.

options.text: Award to the incumbent to break the tie
options.why: Tie-breaking does not address possible collusion.

options.text: Ignore it if the price matches the IGCE
options.why: A suspicious pattern must be reported regardless of price.

stem: An organizational conflict of interest (OCI) exists when:

options.text: A contractor's other work could impair its objectivity or give it an unfair competitive advantage
options.why: OCIs come from unequal access to information, biased ground rules or impaired objectivity.

options.text: A contractor employee also works a second job
options.why: That alone is not an organizational conflict.

options.text: Two offerors rent space in the same building
options.why: Sharing a building does not create an OCI.

options.text: A prime contractor uses a small business subcontractor
options.why: Subcontracting is normal and encouraged.

stem: What must a contract file do?

options.text: Comprehensively record the transaction history so the decisions and support are clear
options.why: The file must give a complete background and support for actions, reviews and litigation.

options.text: Contain only signed documents
options.why: Analyses, memos and correspondence are part of the story too.

options.text: Be destroyed after award to protect information
options.why: Files are kept for set retention periods.

options.text: Be kept by the contractor
options.why: The Government keeps its own contract files.

stem: What is a determination and findings (D&F)?

options.text: A written approval in which the findings (facts) support the determination (decision)
options.why: A D&F is a special form of written approval the FAR requires for certain actions.

options.text: A kind of contract modification
options.why: Modifications use the SF 30.

options.text: A letter that debriefs an unsuccessful offeror
options.why: Debriefings are separate notices.

options.text: GAO's decision on a protest
options.why: GAO issues protest decisions, not D&Fs.

stem: On a noncommercial buy under the simplified acquisition threshold, what is needed to solicit only one source?

options.text: A determination and findings that only one source is reasonably available
options.why: The RFO FAR 13.101(b) requires a D&F to solicit a single source.

options.text: A justification approved by the competition advocate
options.why: Part 6 justifications are for buys above the SAT.

options.text: Nothing; simplified buys need no documentation
options.why: Single-source decisions must be documented.

options.text: Approval from GAO
options.why: GAO does not approve sole-source decisions.

stem: On a phone call, you and a contractor agree that a delivery date should move. What comes next?

options.text: A written record and, because the contract changes, a modification signed by the contracting officer
options.why: Contract changes must be in writing by a contracting officer; the file must show what happened.

options.text: Nothing, since both sides agreed
options.why: Verbal agreements leave the contract unchanged and the file incomplete.

options.text: An email to the COR only
options.why: The COR cannot change the contract, and an email is not a modification.

options.text: A note in CPARS
options.why: CPARS records performance; it does not change contracts.

stem: Where does the Army keep contract files electronically?

options.text: In the Virtual Contracting Enterprise (VCE) Paperless Contract File
options.why: AFARS directs Army contract files into VCE's Paperless Contract File.

options.text: In SAM.gov
options.why: SAM.gov holds registrations, notices and award data, not contract files.

options.text: In PIEE Wide Area WorkFlow
options.why: WAWF handles invoices and receiving reports.

options.text: In GFEBS
options.why: GFEBS is the Army's financial system.

stem: Capturing lessons learned after an acquisition mainly helps the team to:

options.text: Improve future acquisitions and avoid repeating problems
options.why: Situational assessment includes capturing and sharing lessons for future contracts.

options.text: Replace the documentation the file requires
options.why: Lessons learned add to, not replace, required documentation.

options.text: Justify a sole-source award
options.why: Sole-source awards need their own justification.

options.text: Meet Prompt Payment Act deadlines
options.why: Lessons learned are unrelated to payment deadlines.

stem: Acceptance is final and conclusive EXCEPT for:

options.text: Latent defects, fraud, gross mistakes amounting to fraud, or as the contract otherwise provides
options.why: Those are the exceptions to the finality of acceptance.

options.text: Any defect found within one year
options.why: There is no general one-year exception; a warranty might create one.

options.text: Patent defects that inspection would have found
options.why: Patent defects are what inspection is meant to catch before acceptance.

options.text: Defects the COR reports later
options.why: Who reports a defect does not change finality.

stem: Under f.o.b. origin terms, when does the risk of loss pass to the Government?

options.text: When the seller delivers the goods to the carrier at the origin
options.why: Under f.o.b. origin the Government bears the risk during transportation.

options.text: When the goods arrive at destination
options.why: That is f.o.b. destination.

options.text: When the invoice is paid
options.why: Payment timing does not move risk of loss.

options.text: When the Government inspects the goods
options.why: Inspection does not determine when risk passes under f.o.b. terms.

stem: Which is an excusable delay under 52.249-14?

options.text: Unusually severe weather the contractor could not control
options.why: Severe weather beyond the contractor's control and without its fault is listed as excusable.

options.text: The contractor's key employee quits
options.why: Staffing problems are within the contractor's control.

options.text: The contractor underbid the job
options.why: A bad bid is the contractor's own risk.

options.text: A subcontractor the contractor chose is late without any excuse
options.why: A subcontractor's unexcused delay is generally not excusable for the prime.

stem: The Prompt Payment Act generally requires the Government to pay within:

options.text: 30 days after receiving a proper invoice or accepting the work, whichever is later
options.why: That is the standard due date; late payments earn interest automatically.

options.text: 10 days after delivery
options.why: Ten days is not the general rule.

options.text: 60 days after delivery
options.why: The standard is 30 days from the later of a proper invoice or acceptance.

options.text: 90 days after the invoice
options.why: Ninety days would trigger interest under the Act.

stem: After the contracting officer issues a change order under the Changes clause, the contractor must:

options.text: Keep performing the work as changed while any adjustment is worked out
options.why: The duty to proceed applies to properly issued change orders.

options.text: Stop work until the price of the change is agreed
options.why: Stopping work would breach the duty to proceed.

options.text: Refuse any change it has not priced
options.why: Changes within the general scope can be ordered unilaterally.

options.text: Get the COR's approval first
options.why: The COR has no role in authorizing changes.

stem: Why would the Government include a warranty in a contract?

options.text: To keep remedies for defects after acceptance
options.why: A warranty survives acceptance and gives the Government a remedy.

options.text: To replace inspection before acceptance
options.why: Warranties supplement inspection; they do not replace it.

options.text: Because warranties are always free
options.why: Warranties have a cost, so they should be worth it.

options.text: To extend the delivery date
options.why: Warranties are unrelated to delivery schedules.
